1:
The first word is disputed. Ellicott reports opinion much divided whether it means a summary or the chief point, both well supported by usage; he prefers the second, because the phrase joined to it speaks of things being said, and because the following words are no summary. Robertson agrees, calling it the main matter, the pith, though it can also mean a sum of money. Gill offers both senses without choosing between them. Calvin explains why a marker was needed: the argument runs through varied reasonings, and this admonition keeps the reader attentive to what is in view — that Christ’s priesthood is celestial, so that the priesthood established under Moses was made void, being earthly.

Chrysostom alone raises the difficulty. To sit at the right hand is not the office of a priest but of the one the priest serves; and the epistle had earlier separated the two, asking whether the angels are not all ministering spirits, and observing that it is not said to them, Sit thou on my right hand, since he that sitteth is not a minister. How then is he here called a minister, and a minister of the sanctuary? The answer he gives is a rule of the whole epistle: Paul mixes lowly things with lofty in imitation of his Master, so that the lowly become the path to the lofty, and among the great things we learn that the lowly were a condescension. Cyril of Jerusalem takes the session by itself and gathers the testimonies, from Matthew, from Peter, and from the letters to the Romans, Ephesians, Colossians and Hebrews. Calvin reads the ascension as removing both the reproach of the cross and the abject condition assumed with our flesh, so that the priesthood’s dignity is measured by the power that appeared in the resurrection. Henry sees there the reward of the humiliation, and Wesley marks the timing: he sat down, having finished his oblation.

What he is minister of divides them three ways. Barnes says the Greek may mean either holy things or the sanctuary, and holds the connexion to require the most holy place, of which the inner room was the emblem. Ellicott finds the decision difficult but reaches the same result, since the usage of the epistle suggests a place and both expressions occur together in the next chapter; the sanctuary is thus the counterpart of the Holiest and the true tabernacle of the Tent, the one being the place of God’s presence and the other of his appointed service. Calvin decides the other way: the word is neuter, and it is better to take it of the holy duties of the priest, afterwards specified when gifts and sacrifices are mentioned, than of the sanctuary. Gill adds a third, that it may mean the holy ones, the saints to whom Christ ministers in all three offices. Robertson declines the distinction, rendering it of the holy places without separating holy from most holy. Clarke works from the other noun, tracing minister to the words for public and for work: the priest was the servant of the public, and Christ transacts the business of the whole human race; our word liturgy comes from the same root.

The true tabernacle is read almost unanimously, and then not quite. Clarke, Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson all take it of heaven or its ideal sanctuary, Clarke adding that the Jewish tabernacle was man’s work though built by God’s direction while this is God’s work alone, and Robertson that the earthly tent was a symbol the temple merely copied. Wesley breaks from them, suggesting that the true tabernacle may be Christ’s human nature, of which the old tabernacle was the type. Calvin raises the objection the word invites, whether the tabernacle Moses built was then a false one, and answers that true here is set not against what is false but against what is typical.
3:
The rule about sacrifice is turned into an argument. Calvin states the syllogism: the Law appointed priests to offer, so a priesthood without a sacrifice is an empty name; Christ had no such sacrifice; therefore his priesthood is not earthly but of a more excellent character. From the same premise he draws a rule of prayer: since no favour comes from God except through a sacrifice, those who pass by Christ and rush into his presence are guilty of a fatal audacity. Barnes draws a polemical inference: if a priest is by definition one who offers sacrifice, the name belongs to none not appointed to offer, and so not to gospel ministers, the great sacrifice having been offered once and not repeated — the New Testament, he says, never gives them the name. Clarke distinguishes the two words, gifts acknowledging God’s benevolence and sacrifices confessing the ruin sin works, and concludes that Christ at the right hand has offered and offers still. Ellicott leaves it open, allowing either a continued ministration in heaven or simply the rule that every high priest must have something to present.

Why he could not be a priest on earth is answered two ways. Barnes, Clarke and Robertson point to the tribe: the office was already filled, and Christ, not being of Levi, could not officiate. Ellicott expressly distinguishes his own reading. He prefers the older manuscripts, which give: If then He were on earth, He would not even be a priest, seeing there are those who according to law offer the gifts. The earlier argument turned on tribe; here the place is preoccupied by men commanded to bring the gifts. Wesley reads it the same way. Calvin prefers a rendering of his own, He could not be a priest as long as there are priests who offer, to the version making him merely not one of their number. Clarke draws a date from it: the temple service was evidently still performed, which he takes as proof that the epistle preceded the fall of Jerusalem. Gill answers a different opponent: the Socinians argue from this verse that Christ was neither priest nor sacrificer on earth, whereas his coming was in the character of a priest and his death his sacrifice, offered before he entered heaven. Calvin secures the point by a distinction: Christ died on earth, but his death’s virtue proceeded from heaven.

The words for copy and shadow are weighed, and two reject the received construction. Barnes explains the first as a copy and the second by the nature of a shadow, which gives form and outline and size but has no substance. Ellicott makes the copy no perfect resemblance but a token designed to suggest the original, and warns that these words must not be confounded with the pattern named later. Clarke and Calvin both object to the English. Clarke calls it absurd to make the priests serve unto a representation of heavenly things, since they served rather unto the substance, with representations and shadows; Calvin reaches the same place, taking the verb of performing sacred rites with a preposition understood, against the rendering which makes them serve the shadow itself.

The pattern in the mount closes the span. Clarke thinks God very likely gave Moses a regular plan and specification of the tabernacle. Robertson notes that the word is the one used in Exodus and quoted by Stephen, and that the verb rendered warned does not name God, though God is meant. Calvin makes it an anticipated objection: the ancient worship was not superfluous, since it referred to something higher, even heavenly realities. Wesley draws it out in a figure: the pattern is like strokes pencilled on fine linen which show leaves and flowers before their colours are laid on, and the shadow gives a dim idea of the body without its living graces, yet both lead the mind to something nobler.
6:
The comparison is stated and measured. Barnes describes the ministry as a service of a higher order, the substance of which the other was the emblem, pertaining to heaven while the older was concerned with the earthly tabernacle, and enduring while that was to vanish. Calvin explains why both were needed: the Jews had to be led away from a superstitious observance of rituals, and Moses and Aaron rightly gave way, the gospel being a more excellent covenant and Christ’s death a nobler sacrifice than the victims of the Law. Henry makes the distinction a first principle, that the body and soul of all divinity consists very much in rightly distinguishing the covenant of works from the covenant of grace and the two dispensations of the latter from each other; he sets the old at Sinai, with Moses as mediator, and calls it a dispensation of darkness and dread.

The verb rendered established draws attention. Ellicott would render it ordained, since the word properly means to legislate and has already been used of the people receiving the Law, so that a term for passing a law is applied to a covenant; the explanation lies in the nature of God’s covenants, not compacts between equals but arrangements offered on conditions, which may therefore be spoken of as enacted upon the basis of promise. Robertson renders it enacted; Calvin fixes the sense as what is set as a law, firmly and irrevocably. Barnes works on the noun, observing that the word used properly denotes a disposition or ordering of things and that the ordinary Greek word for a compact is never used. On what makes them better, Clarke sets the old covenant’s earthly things and secular good against the new covenant’s spiritual and eternal blessings, and Wesley points to the verses that specify them, the promises of the law being mostly temporal. Calvin and Robertson both stop at the difficulty: it is not obvious how promises can be better if the earlier were also from God.

What was faulty in the first covenant is answered carefully. Barnes denies that it had any real fault, and locates the defect in what it lacked, ample provision for pardon, it being merely preparatory. Clarke and Wesley argue from the fact of a second: had the first conferred pardon and a title to life, or answered all God’s designs and man’s wants, there could have been no room for another. Ellicott says the failure was manifest to God, who sought place for a second while the first still stood; Robertson calls the assumption a serious charge which the writer hastens to explain.

Calvin alone turns the difficulty into an objection and answers it. It seems hardly consistent, he says, that one who has just argued that no place would have been sought for a second had the first been faultless should then say the people were at fault; it seems unjust that blame lying in the people should be transferred to God’s covenant, and the argument seems invalid, since God might blame the people a hundred times without the covenant being faulty. His answer is that both are true at once: the crime of violating it was justly imputed to a people who had departed from God, and yet the weakness of the covenant is also pointed out, since it was not written where it would hold. Gill guards the verse differently, distinguishing this first covenant from two it might be confused with. It is not the covenant of works, made in paradise with Adam and his posterity, without mediator or forgiveness, whereas this was made at Sinai with the Jews through Moses and dedicated with blood; nor the covenant of grace as now administered, which though made first is second in administration, reaches the Gentiles, is of pure grace and everlasting, whereas this was made with good and bad, required works, and is done away.
8:
With whom the fault is found divides them, and Barnes maps the division. One party, he reports, takes the complaint to be with the covenant itself rather than with the people, who had no hand in giving it, naming Stuart, Rosenmuller and Erasmus; another, naming Doddridge and Koppe, follows the English version in finding the fault with the people, and appeals to Jeremiah. The Greek, he says, will bear either. He then offers a third reading, that the writer found fault specifically with neither, but used language of complaint implying a defect somewhere when he promised a better covenant. Ellicott decides for the people, not with it but with those through whom the covenant had failed; Robertson states it baldly, that the covenant was all right but the Jews failed to keep it, so God made a new one of grace in place of law. Gill and Clarke will not choose, finding fault with the covenant, which had its faults, and with the people, who kept it not.

Calvin raises a different objection, that the apostle seems to turn the prophecy unreasonably to his own purpose: the question here is of ceremonies while the prophet speaks of the whole Law. His answer is that the argument runs from the whole to a part. The prophet includes the whole Mosaic dispensation when he says the covenant was not kept; and the Law was in a manner clothed with ceremonies, so that when the body is dead there is no use for garments, the accessory being of the same character as its principal. No wonder, then, that ceremonies, mere appendages of the old covenant, should end.

Who is promised the new covenant is answered two ways. Clarke takes the two houses for all the descendants of the twelve sons of Jacob, and reports that the words are thought to promise the conversion of all the Jews, the lost tribes included. Wesley reads it of all the Israel of God in all ages and nations, and sets out how the covenant is new though not new in substance: ratified by the death of Christ, freed from burdensome rites, fuller in its account of spiritual religion, attended with larger influences of the Spirit, extended to all men, and never to be abolished. Robertson adds that the word for new means fresh and on new lines, not merely young.

The last clause exposes a divergence between apostle and prophet, and those who notice it react differently. Clarke is scandalised: the Hebrew says God was a husband to them, the apostle that he regarded them not, and if the English is correct he asks how such a difference can be accounted for, and whether the Spirit of God could be the author of what looks like a contradiction. Ellicott states the same fact without alarm: here the translation departs from the Hebrew, which is now generally believed to be faithfully represented by the English rendering about a husband, the quotation following the Greek version without change. Calvin notices that the prophet expresses something more in Hebrew and sets it aside as little to the present question, taking the clause to mean that it would have profited them nothing to have been once adopted unless God succoured them by this new remedy. Robertson keeps to the Greek, that the covenant was void when they broke it. On the clause before it they agree: Calvin says the mention of God laying hold on their hand enhances the sin of defection by recalling so great a benefit, and that not one age only is charged, since those delivered fell away at once and their posterity after them, so that the whole nation had become covenant-breakers; Wesley puts the same in a phrase, that God took them with the care of a parent, and that while it was fresh in memory they obeyed and presently shook off the yoke.
10:
The parties and timing are settled first. Gill and Barnes take the house of Israel spiritually, of the chosen people or the true Israel whom God treats as his friends; Ellicott explains the single name historically, that once the reunion of the nation had been signified Israel could stand alone for the one people. Barnes notes that the phrase about those days may attach either to the covenant or to the putting of the laws, a matter of punctuation, but thinks the Hebrew means in those after days, and refers it to the times of the Messiah; Wesley dates it from the abolition of the Mosaic dispensation, Clarke from the times of the Gospel.

What the writing on the heart effects is pressed furthest by Calvin. Ellicott contrasts the fleshy tablets of the heart with the tables of the Law, notes that the Hebrew has the law in their inward parts, and calls this the first of the better promises. Clarke fills it out, that the understanding shall be enlightened and the affections purified, so that men obey willingly and feel that love fulfils the law; Wesley, that they shall inwardly experience what God commands. Calvin turns the promise into an argument. God calls us without effect so long as he speaks only by the voice of man, for he speaks to the deaf, our ears struck by an empty sound while the heart rejects every wholesome doctrine; the word never penetrates hearts of iron and stone until he softens them, a contrary law being engraven there already. In vain does God proclaim his Law by a human voice unless he writes it by his Spirit; and from this, he says, it appears what freewill and natural uprightness are worth before God regenerates us.

What the promise about teaching abolishes is the sharpest question here. Clarke answers from institutions. Under the old covenant there was properly no public instruction: worship was confined to the tabernacle and then the temple, the synagogues served mainly for the bare reading of the law, and scarcely any continual ministry to the common people existed until John the Baptist and the apostles, the prophets not reaching all and the rabbinic schools being for select persons. Hence every man had then to instruct his neighbour, whereas the prophecy promises a profusion of divine light in the plentiful diffusion of the Scriptures and an abundant ministry, found in every corner of the land. Gill answers from another anxiety, denying that the words set aside either the public ministry, a standing ordinance, or the private instruction Christians owe each other; the sense is that the Spirit should teach with men and by them, the promise standing against pretended revelations and above all against magisterial dictates. Barnes takes it of necessity rather than practice, that none shall be obliged to impart the knowledge of God to another, quoting Doddridge that they shall have a more certain teaching than any derived from a fellow man; and he warns that the promise is not of a universally diffused religion but of exact knowledge among those who share the covenant. Robertson makes the contrast one of learning, since under the old covenant only the trained scribe could master the minutiae of the law. Wesley concedes openly that in other respects they will need to teach one another to their lives’ end.

Two notes close the span. Ellicott would read fellow-citizen rather than neighbour, and calls the universal knowledge of God the second promise. On the order from the least to the greatest, Calvin finds grace poured on all ranks so that no class is without it, while Wesley insists on the sequence itself, that saving knowledge ever did and ever will proceed so and never first to the greatest, citing the promise that the Lord will save the tents of Judah first so that the house of David does not magnify itself.
12:
Where the promise of pardon stands is counted three ways. Ellicott calls it the third and chief promise, the covenant being ordained on three: an inward revelation, a universal knowledge of God, and free forgiveness. Barnes counts differently, making it the fourth circumstance in which the new covenant surpasses the old; the older system contemplated pardon and made arrangements for it, but mercy was not its crowning attribute, and what distinguishes the gospel from every other system is that it both provides forgiveness and actually bestows it. Wesley reverses the order and makes pardon first, not in the text but in experience: justification is the root of all true knowledge of God, and this is God’s method — a sinner is pardoned, then knows God as gracious and merciful, then has the laws written on his heart.

The word rendered merciful and those governed by it are examined. Gill, Ellicott and Robertson agree that it means propitious, Robertson noting that it is an old Attic adjective found nowhere else in the New Testament, from which the verb for making propitiation comes. Gill presses the sense: God pardons none but those to whom he has been rendered propitious by Christ, so that forgiveness is an act of justice as well as of mercy. Clarke reaches the same by the covenant sacrifice, and expounds the three nouns as a graded account of evil — unrighteousness, injustice against God, neighbour and self; sin, deviation from the divine law, a missing of the mark by those who seek happiness outside God; and iniquity, lawlessness, having no law written in the heart. Ellicott quietly removes the ground of that third member, reporting that the best authorities omit the words about iniquities and rendering the verse of unrighteousnesses and sins alone. He adds that the pardon is spoken of not as a gift to individuals but as from the first a property of the covenant, difficulties having arisen from forgetting that no sudden change in man’s relation to God is in view.

The last verse is read as an argument from the word new. Barnes and Robertson make it a matter of contradistinction: new and old stand over against each other, so that calling the second covenant new is to treat the first as out of date. Calvin puts the inference more formally, that establishing one covenant subverts the other, and offers his own rendering: by saying a new covenant he has made ancient the first, and what is ancient and grows old is nigh a dissolution. All three then reach for the same figure. Barnes lists an old house, an old garment, an ancient tree and an aged man, each with its sign that it will soon disappear; Calvin has an old man tottering on the brink of the grave, who once buried disappears from among the living; Robertson notes that the second verb belongs to the decay of age.

How near the vanishing was becomes a question about the date. Clarke says the apostle intimates that the old covenant was about to be abolished, but expresses himself cautiously so as to give no offence; he supports the word from Dionysius of Halicarnassus, who used it of the laws of Numa, written on oak boards, which had perished through old age. Wesley answers that it vanished quickly after, when the temple was destroyed, and Calvin that an intimation is supposed of the dissolution of the whole Jewish polity, which soon took place. Robertson turns the tense into evidence: the writer writes as though the ceremonial system were about to vanish, and if he had written after the fall of Jerusalem, would he not have said that it had vanished? Clarke closes by supporting the earlier promise from the rabbins, citing a saying that in the days of the Messiah knowledge shall be renewed in the world and the law made plain among all.
